name: Burgruine Vilsegg
kurzbeschreibung: Burgruine Vilsegg near Vils in the Außerfern: built around 1220 by the Herren von Hohenegg, significant Hohenstaufen hilltop castle with 17 m high rusticated ashlar keep.
beschreibung:
Overview

The historic Burgruine Vilsegg rises atop a prominent wooded rock cone, the Schlossberg, at approximately 987 metres above sea level just southwest of the border town of Vils in the Tyrolean Außerfern. Nestled within the mountain landscape of the Tannheimer Berge near the Bavarian border at Füssen, this hilltop castle ruin is considered the oldest and architecturally most significant Hohenstaufen fortification in the entire district of Reutte. With its monumental, far-visible keep (Bergfried) made of light Romanesque rusticated ashlars (Buckelquader) and sweeping views over the Vilstal valley, the ruin represents a rewarding destination for culture enthusiasts and hikers alike.

History & Architecture

The fortress was constructed in the first half of the 13th century (around 1220/1230) by the noble Herren von Hohenegg, who originally hailed from the Allgäu and served as loyal ministeriales to the Prince-Bishopric of Kempten (Hochstift Kempten) and the Diocese of Augsburg (Bistum Augsburg). At this strategically vital border stronghold, the Hoheneggs installed their own ministerials, who took their name from the castle (first documented in 1263 with Heinrich von Vilsegg). The castle served to secure imperial hunting and forestry rights and to guard nearby medieval trade routes connected to the Via Claudia Augusta. In 1408, the Hoheneggs ceded the castle to the Tyrolean sovereign Duke Friedrich IV. Following the extinction of the Hohenegg line around 1540 and the relocation of the court of justice, the fortification lost its military purpose and fell into ruin from the 18th century onwards. In architectural history, Vilsegg represents an exemplary model of Hohenstaufen military architecture: the monumental, nearly square Bergfried measures roughly 10 by 11 metres at its base and stands to a preserved height of around 17 metres. Its outer walls consist of carefully dressed, heavy Buckelquader aus hellem Wettersteinkalk (rusticated ashlar blocks of light Wetterstein limestone) with precise drafted margins. During a severe earthquake in the Außerfern on 8 October 1939, the eastern wall of the tower with its elevated entrance collapsed. In the 1990s and 2000s, the keep and curtain walls underwent extensive structural stabilization supported by the Messerschmitt-Stiftung and the Land Tirol. At the foot of the rock stand the Gothic St.-Anna-Kirche and the historic Hammerschmiede of the Hoheneggs.

Visit & Arrival

The Burgruine Vilsegg is freely accessible year-round, 365 days a year, around the clock, and is completely free of charge (€0.00 admission). There are no gates or turnstiles at the historic walls (in winter, the forest trail is snow-covered and requires caution). Public transport arrival: Take the Außerfernbahn (ÖBB/DB) directly to Bahnhof Vils; from there, walk approx. 30 minutes through the historic town of Vils and up the signposted Burgweg to the ruin. By car: From Tirol via the B179 Fernpassstraße and B198 to Vils, or toll-free from Bavaria via the A7/B310; free parking options are located directly in the town centre of Vils or at the hiker car park by the St.-Anna-Kirche at the foot of the Schlossberg.

Tips

The ascent from the valley car park to the ruin takes only around 15 to 20 minutes (approx. 100 metres of elevation gain), but follows a narrow, stony forest path with exposed roots and is therefore not barrier-free (unsuitable for wheelchairs and strollers); sturdy walking boots are recommended. Combine your hike to the ruin with a tour of the heritage-listed Historischen Hammerschmiede (hammer mill) in the valley and a stop for refreshments at the traditional Gutshof Schluxen. Ambitious hikers can extend the excursion to the romantic Alatsee lake and onward to the Salober Alm on the Austrian-German border.
